name: Sub-conscious Burger - on a sub roll

recipe.history:
The sub roll — known variously as a hoagie roll, hero roll, grinder roll, or Italian roll depending on the American region — descends directly from the long, crusty breads of southern Italy, particularly the pane di casa and filone loaves of Naples, Calabria, and Sicily. Italian immigrants arriving in the United States between 1880 and 1920 brought with them the tradition of stuffed bread — meats, cheeses, and pickled vegetables packed into sturdy rolls designed to hold up under the weight and moisture of their fillings without disintegrating. The sub sandwich as a distinct American form is generally traced to Philadelphia, New York, and New England in the early twentieth century, with Italian delis and corner stores serving torpedo-shaped rolls stuffed with salami, provolone, roasted peppers, and oil as working-class lunches for dockworkers, factory hands, and construction crews. The name "submarine" reportedly came from the bread's resemblance to the long, low silhouette of a Navy submarine — a comparison that various cities claim to have coined first and none can definitively prove. By the mid-twentieth century, chains like Subway, Blimpie, and Jersey Mike's had standardized the sub roll into a national institution, though the best iterations remain the hand-formed, sesame-seeded Italian rolls from independent bakeries in Boston, Philadelphia, and New York.

The idea of putting a burger on a sub roll rather than a round bun is a deliberate act of genre-crossing that reflects the particular genius of Bob's Burgers — taking a format everyone knows and slightly, productively violating it. Sub rolls are structurally different from burger buns in ways that matter: they have more crumb volume to absorb juices without becoming soggy, a thicker crust that provides resistance and crunch, and a longer format that changes the bite geometry of the burger entirely. Instead of a round, symmetrical bite where all components are compressed into a uniform disc, a sub roll burger gives you a linear eating experience — each bite may hit a slightly different combination of toppings, the way a real sub sandwich does. The Italian bread also invites Italian-inflected toppings: giardiniera, pickled peppers, oregano oil, provolone, shaved iceberg. Placing a beef patty inside a sub roll is not just a novelty. It is a genuine reimagining of what a burger can be.

The sub roll entered my cooking life through a very specific and unglamorous route: I was nineteen, broke, and living near a bakery that sold day-old Italian rolls for almost nothing. I would buy a bag of them and fill them with whatever was around — canned tuna, leftover ground beef, scrambled eggs. The rolls were the best part. Even day-old, they had a chew and a faint yeasty sourness that supermarket burger buns couldn't touch. I started buying them fresh and making what I called burgers on sub rolls, though I didn't yet understand that I was doing something with genuine culinary logic. Years later, when I started thinking carefully about bread and its relationship to what it holds, I understood what those cheap Italian rolls were teaching me: that bread is not a passive container but an active contributor to flavor and texture, and that the best bread for a burger depends entirely on the burger's character. A sub roll burger is louder and more assertive than a brioche burger. It has opinions.

Medium rare — 130–135°F (54–57°C) — is especially critical on a sub roll because of the bread's greater structural integrity. A round brioche bun will compress around a medium rare patty, distributing the juices evenly as you press down. A sub roll has a firm crust that does not compress in the same way, which means the burger's juices need to be internal — held within the patty itself — rather than spread through the bun. An overcooked patty on a sub roll is a dry patty on a cracker, with nowhere for the flavor to go. A medium rare patty on a sub roll is a juicy core inside a crunchy shell, and every bite releases a small flood of savory beef fat that soaks slightly into the bread's crumb and makes the whole thing cohere. The Maillard crust on the outside of the patty also has more visible real estate on a sub roll — you see the entire browned exterior — which means there is no hiding an improperly cooked burger. Medium rare is the truth this bread demands.
ingredients: 1.5 lbs (680g) ground beef, 80/20 chuck, freshly ground
4 Italian sub rolls (8 inches long, sesame-seeded preferred), split lengthwise
2 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil (for toasting rolls)
3 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil (for dressing)
1/2 small head iceberg lettuce, finely shredded
1/2 red onion, thinly sliced into rings
1/4 cup Chicago-style giardiniera, chopped (mild or hot, your preference)
instructions: 1. Make the Italian dressing: whisk together red wine vinegar, dried oregano, grated garlic, and crushed red pepper flakes. Slowly whisk in 3 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil until emulsified. Season with salt and pepper. Set aside.
2. Make the oregano mayo: stir 1 teaspoon dried oregano and a pinch of red pepper flakes into the mayonnaise. Refrigerate until needed.
3. Combine ground beef, kosher salt, black pepper, dried oregano, garlic powder, fennel seeds, and Worcestershire sauce in a large bowl. Mix gently with your hands until just combined.

4. Divide the mixture into 4 equal portions (approximately 6 oz / 170g each). Form into oval-shaped patties that roughly match the width of your sub rolls — about 4 inches long and 3/4 inch thick. Press a slight dimple in the center. Refrigerate for at least 20 minutes.
5. Heat a cast iron skillet or heavy ridged grill pan over high heat until smoking. Brush lightly with neutral oil.
6. Season the outside of each patty with flaky salt. Cook for 3–4 minutes on the first side without moving, until a deep crust forms.

7. Flip each patty. Lay one slice of provolone on each. Add the tablespoon of butter to the pan and baste briefly. Cover loosely with a lid or foil tent and cook 2–3 more minutes until an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center reads 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare.
8. Transfer patties to a wire rack and rest for 3–4 minutes.

9. While patties rest, brush the cut sides of the sub rolls with extra virgin olive oil. Toast cut-side down in the skillet over medium heat, or under a broiler, for 2–3 minutes until golden and slightly crunchy on the surface.
10. Toss the shredded iceberg with 1–2 tablespoons of the Italian dressing to lightly coat.
11. Assemble each sub burger: spread oregano mayo on both cut sides of the roll. Lay the dressed iceberg on the bottom half. Add tomato slices, red onion rings, and a basil leaf.
12. Place the rested patty with melted provolone on top of the vegetables. Add a spoonful of giardiniera and several pepperoncini slices. If using mortadella, tuck a torn piece alongside the patty.
13. Drizzle a small amount of the remaining Italian dressing directly over the patty and toppings. Press the top of the roll down firmly and serve immediately, cut in half on the diagonal.
